summary: Defines the 607 (Unwanted) SIP response code. A called party can use it to say a call or message was unwanted, and SIP entities may use the information to change how future calls from that caller are handled.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone calls you with a sales pitch, you can press a button that tells the phone company you did not want it.

questions: how to report unwanted sip calls
what does sip response 607 unwanted mean
what is the sip.607 feature capability
subtitle: A new SIP response code that lets a called party say a call or message was unwanted.

tldr.problem: None of the existing SIP 4xx, 5xx or 6xx response codes say that a request is unwanted by the called party, so providers get no in-call feedback about unwanted calls.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the 607 (Unwanted) response code, which a called party's user agent can send to reject a request or can cite in a Reason header field when it ends a call.
tldr.outcome: Service providers may use 607 as one input to call-filtering algorithms, but the RFC does not require any particular action and leaves the filtering itself out of scope.

today: RFC 8197 is a Proposed Standard from July 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Unwanted Calls and SIP Feedback
sections.content:
Many countries see a growing number of unwanted calls. They may be fraudulent or illegal telemarketing, or just surveys and solicitations the receiver does not want. Carriers and other service providers may want to help subscribers avoid them, and one input into their filtering is feedback from users.

User feedback can come through smartphone apps, APIs or inside a SIP-initiated call. RFC 8197 covers only the last case. The called party either rejects the SIP request as unwanted, or ends the session with a BYE request after answering. INVITE and MESSAGE requests are the most likely triggers.

To express this, the RFC defines the 607 (Unwanted) response code. The called party's user agent (UA) uses it, based on user input or its own logic, to say that the call is unwanted and that future attempts are likely to be rejected the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a way to tell the phone network, in the middle of a call, 'this caller is a pest.'

sections.title: Why 603 Is Not Enough
sections.content:
None of the existing 4xx, 5xx or 6xx codes signify that a request is unwanted by the called party. The closest is 603 (Decline), which might be used when the called party is at dinner or in a meeting and does not want to give a reason. A 603 may carry a Retry-After header field suggesting a better time to call, so it describes the callee's temporary status.

A 607 says something different: it is the caller's identity that causes the rejection. The called party triggers it through an 'unwanted call' user interface.

In this RFC, 'identity' means either a canonical address-of-record SIP URI such as sip:alice@atlanta.example.com, or a telephone number, which usually appears in a tel URI or as the user part of a SIP URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying 'not now, I am at dinner' is different from saying 'I never want calls from you.' 607 is the second one.

sections.title: How 607 Is Used
sections.content:
The 607 code MAY be used in a failure response to an INVITE, MESSAGE, SUBSCRIBE or other out-of-dialog SIP request. It MAY also be used as the cause parameter of a reason-value in a Reason header field (RFC 3326). That is typical when the called UA sends a BYE to end an incoming call, or when a forking proxy sends a CANCEL after one branch returns 607. The Reason header lets the UA receiving a CANCEL decide whether and how to list the call as missed.

Entities that receive 607 do not have to do anything beyond what is normal for 6xx responses. Following the default 6xx handling in RFC 5057, a 607 response destroys the transaction.

The provider delivering calls to the user MAY act on it. Examples in the text are adding the caller to a personal blacklist for that user, using it as input to the likelihood that the caller places unwanted calls ('crowd sourcing'), starting a traceback request, or reporting the caller to consumer complaint databases. Reversing an 'unwanted' label is outside the mechanism, since it likely needs something other than call signaling.

The user experience is envisioned to be somewhat like an email spam button, where the provider's detailed actions stay opaque to the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Pressing the button is like telling the school 'this person keeps bothering me.' The school then decides what to do.

sections.title: Using 607 in Call Filtering
sections.content:
The 607 response is only one of many inputs a provider is likely to use. Call handling is likely to combine heuristics, analytics and machine learning, using call duration, call volumes and changes over time, plus user feedback from non-SIP routes and from this mechanism. Implementations must trade off falsely labeling a caller as unwanted against delivering unwanted calls. The heuristics and treatment of persistent offenders are outside the scope of the RFC.

Some details the RFC points out:

  • Systems may treat pre-call and mid-call responses differently, since in a mid-call rejection the called party has already seen the call content.
  • A 607 does not necessarily block all calls from that identity. The same user action might add the caller to a local, on-device blacklist or graylist, for example to flag calls with a different ring tone.
  • The same anonymous SIP URI (RFC 3323) may be used by many callers, so such URIs are unlikely to suit URI-specific treatment. Entities tallying responses may need to canonicalize SIP URIs and telephone numbers.
  • The caller may appear in the From header field, P-Asserted-Identity or History-Info, and diverting services can complicate this.
sections.plainLanguage: One complaint is only a hint. The phone company mixes many hints, like how many calls someone makes, before it decides to block them.

sections.title: Advertising Support with sip.607
sections.content:
The RFC defines a SIP feature-capability (RFC 6809) named sip.607. It lets the registrar indicate that the corresponding proxy supports the 607 response code. A UA can then show a suitable control, such as a 'spam' button, only if its service provider supports the feature.

The capability does not promise any action, such as blocking future calls. A UA may still show a spam button without it, for example if it keeps a device-local blacklist or reports unwanted calls to a third party.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company can tell your phone 'yes, we understand the spam button,' so the button only shows up when it will be heard.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC adds response code 607 with the description Unwanted to the 'Response Codes' subregistry of the 'Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Parameters' registry.

It also registers the feature-capability indicator sip.607 in the 'SIP Feature-Capability Indicator Registration Tree' defined by RFC 6809. When it appears in a Feature-Caps header field of a REGISTER response, it indicates that the server supports and will process the 607 response code.
sections.plainLanguage: The new code and the new 'we support it' label were written into the official lists so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Abuse, Mistakes and Spoofing
sections.content:
If the caller address is spoofed, users may report an identity that is not the real culprit. The legitimate holder of that identity could get blocked, which becomes a form of denial-of-service attack. So 607 SHOULD NOT be used to create global call filters unless the caller identity has been authenticated as belonging to the caller placing the unwanted call.

Even without spoofing, a recipient might flag a legitimate caller out of revenge or by mistake. Additions to a personal block list should be observable and reversible by the protected party, for example shown on a web page or sent as periodic email reminders. Global or carrier-wide lists need to expect an unavoidable rate of false positives, for example by comparing the fraction of delivered calls flagged rather than the absolute number, and by weighting recent feedback more.

An attacker on an unsecured network who can spoof SIP responses for many recipients might make the filter block legitimate calls. Using TLS for signaling mitigates this.

Caller identities are routinely reassigned to new subscribers, so algorithms are advised to check for reassignment and possibly reset the rating. Services such as third party call control (RFC 3725) and call transfer (RFC 5359) make it harder to tell who should be flagged when a 607 arrives in a BYE.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pretend to be your phone number and get you blocked, or press the button out of spite. So the rules say to be careful and let people fix mistakes.

left.title: 603 (Decline)
left.desc: Rejected because of the called party's own, possibly temporary, status.

right.title: 607 (Unwanted)
right.desc: Rejected because the caller's identity itself is unwanted.
